questions.q: Two Sum: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers whose sum equals the target.
questions.a: Use a **hash map** to store each visited number and its index. For every element, check whether `target - current` is already in the map. This gives an **O(n)** solution and is the expected interview answer in JavaScript.

questions.q: Contains Duplicate: Determine whether an array contains any duplicate values.
questions.a: Use a **Set** and compare its size with the array length, or iterate while checking if a value has already been seen. A clean JavaScript solution runs in **O(n)** time with **O(n)** extra space.

questions.q: Valid Anagram: Check whether two strings are anagrams of each other.
questions.a: Count character frequencies with an object or `Map`, then decrement using the second string. If all counts end at zero, the strings are anagrams. Sorting also works but frequency counting is better at **O(n)**.

questions.q: Group Anagrams: Group words that are anagrams into separate arrays.
questions.a: Use the **sorted version** of each word as the grouping key. Store groups inside a `Map<string, string[]>`. This is one of the most common JavaScript interview problems involving hashing and strings.

questions.q: Top K Frequent Elements: Return the `k` most frequent numbers in an array.
questions.a: Count frequencies with a map, then use **bucket sort** or a **min heap**. Bucket sort is often preferred in interviews because it can achieve **O(n)** time when the value range is manageable.

questions.q: Product of Array Except Self: Return an array where each position contains the product of all other elements without using division.
questions.a: Build prefix products from the left and suffix products from the right, then combine them. This avoids division and gives **O(n)** time with **O(1)** extra space excluding the output array.

questions.q: Maximum Subarray: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum.
questions.a: Apply **Kadane's Algorithm**. Track the best running sum ending at the current index and the global maximum. This is a classic interview favorite with **O(n)** time.

questions.q: Maximum Product Subarray: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest product.
questions.a: Track both the current **maximum product** and **minimum product** because a negative number can flip them. Update both values at each step. This is a common extension of Kadane-style reasoning.

questions.q: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock: Find the maximum profit from one buy and one sell.
questions.a: Track the **lowest price seen so far** and the best profit at each step. This yields a simple **O(n)** scan and is a very standard coding-round problem.

questions.q: Container With Most Water: Given heights, find the maximum water container area.
questions.a: Use **two pointers** from both ends. Move the smaller height inward because the smaller side limits the area. This reduces the brute-force **O(n^2)** approach to **O(n)**.

questions.q: 3Sum: Find all unique triplets in an array that sum to zero.
questions.a: Sort the array, then fix one element and use a **two-pointer scan** for the remaining pair. Skip duplicates carefully. This is a high-frequency interview problem and the expected answer is **O(n^2)**.

questions.q: Trapping Rain Water: Calculate how much water can be trapped between bars.
questions.a: Use two pointers with `leftMax` and `rightMax`, or precompute prefix and suffix maxima. The optimized two-pointer solution is **O(n)** time and **O(1)** extra space.

questions.q: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters: Return the length of the longest substring with unique characters.
questions.a: Use a **sliding window** with a map of last seen indices. Move the left pointer whenever a repeated character is found inside the current window. This is a core string interview pattern.

questions.q: Longest Repeating Character Replacement: Replace at most `k` characters to make the longest repeating-character substring.
questions.a: Use a sliding window and track the count of the most frequent character inside the window. If `windowSize - maxFreq > k`, shrink from the left. This puzzle shows up often in interview prep sheets.

questions.q: Minimum Window Substring: Find the smallest substring of `s` that contains all characters of `t`.
questions.a: Use a variable-size **sliding window** with frequency counts for required characters. Expand right until valid, then shrink left to minimize. This is a strong interview-crack-level problem.

questions.q: Valid Palindrome: Check whether a string is a palindrome after removing non-alphanumeric characters and ignoring case.
questions.a: Use **two pointers** from both ends and skip invalid characters while comparing lowercase values. This is a simple but common screening problem.

questions.q: Longest Palindromic Substring: Return the longest palindromic substring in a string.
questions.a: Expand around every character and every gap between characters to handle odd and even lengths. The center-expansion solution is **O(n^2)** and is often enough for interviews.

questions.q: Palindromic Substrings: Count how many substrings of a string are palindromes.
questions.a: Expand around each center and count every valid palindrome found. This is closely related to longest palindromic substring and is a nice follow-up interview puzzle.

questions.q: Encode and Decode Strings: Design a way to serialize and deserialize a list of strings.
questions.a: Store each string with its **length prefix** and a separator, then parse using the length while decoding. This avoids problems with embedded delimiters and is a classic system-style coding question.

questions.q: Reverse Linked List: Reverse a singly linked list iteratively.
questions.a: Keep `prev`, `curr`, and `next` pointers, reversing each link one by one. This is one of the most fundamental linked-list interview questions.

questions.q: Merge Two Sorted Lists: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
questions.a: Use a **dummy node** and compare the heads of both lists while building the merged result. This pattern appears often in linked-list and merge-sort discussions.

questions.q: Linked List Cycle: Detect whether a linked list contains a cycle.
questions.a: Use **Floyd's tortoise and hare** algorithm with slow and fast pointers. If they meet, there is a cycle. This is the expected interview solution with **O(1)** space.

questions.q: Reorder List: Reorder a linked list into `L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 ...`.
questions.a: Find the middle, reverse the second half, then merge the two halves alternately. This combines multiple linked-list techniques and is a strong medium-level interview problem.

questions.q: Remove Nth Node From End of List: Delete the nth node from the end in one pass.
questions.a: Use a **dummy node** and maintain two pointers `n` steps apart. When the fast pointer reaches the end, slow will be just before the node to remove.

questions.q: Merge K Sorted Lists: Merge multiple sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
questions.a: Use a **min heap** to repeatedly take the smallest current node, or apply divide and conquer merging. Heap-based solutions are common in JS using a custom priority queue.

questions.q: Invert Binary Tree: Swap left and right children for every node in a binary tree.
questions.a: Use simple recursion or iterative BFS/DFS. This is a straightforward tree traversal question and often appears in screening rounds.

questions.q: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree: Find the maximum depth of a binary tree.
questions.a: Use recursion to return `1 + max(leftDepth, rightDepth)`, or BFS level traversal. This is one of the most basic tree interview problems.

questions.q: Same Tree: Check whether two binary trees are structurally identical with the same values.
questions.a: Traverse both trees together. If both nodes are null, return true; if only one is null or values differ, return false; otherwise compare both children recursively.

questions.q: Subtree of Another Tree: Determine whether one binary tree is a subtree of another.
questions.a: At each node in the main tree, check whether the subtree rooted there matches the target tree using a helper for exact tree comparison. This is a classic recursive interview question.

questions.q: Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST: Find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a binary search tree.
questions.a: Use the BST ordering rule. If both targets are smaller, go left; if both are larger, go right; otherwise the current node is the answer.

questions.q: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal: Return nodes level by level.
questions.a: Use **BFS** with a queue and process nodes layer by layer. This is one of the most common tree traversal coding questions.

questions.q: Validate Binary Search Tree: Check whether a binary tree is a valid BST.
questions.a: Pass down valid `min` and `max` bounds during recursion, or perform inorder traversal and ensure values are strictly increasing. Bounds-based recursion is very interview-friendly.

questions.q: Kth Smallest Element in a BST: Return the kth smallest node value.
questions.a: Perform **inorder traversal**, because inorder on a BST visits nodes in sorted order. Count visited nodes until reaching `k`.

questions.q: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal.
questions.a: Use preorder to identify the root and inorder to split left and right subtrees. A map from value to inorder index helps reduce repeated searches.

questions.q: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum: Find the maximum path sum across any path in the tree.
questions.a: Use DFS. For each node, compute the best gain from left and right children, ignoring negative contributions, and update a global maximum with `node.val + leftGain + rightGain`.

questions.q: Clone Graph: Deep copy an undirected graph.
questions.a: Use DFS or BFS with a map from original node to cloned node. This avoids duplicating work and handles cycles safely.

questions.q: Number of Islands: Count how many islands are present in a 2D grid.
questions.a: Scan the grid, and every time you find land, run DFS or BFS to mark the entire connected component visited. This is one of the most asked grid problems.

questions.q: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow: Return cells that can flow to both oceans.
questions.a: Instead of starting from every cell, run DFS or BFS **from the ocean borders inward** and mark reachable cells for each ocean. Intersect the two visited sets at the end.

questions.q: Course Schedule: Determine whether all courses can be finished given prerequisites.
questions.a: Model the courses as a directed graph and detect cycles using DFS states or **topological sorting** with indegrees. A cycle means the schedule is impossible.

questions.q: Course Schedule II: Return one valid course order if possible.
questions.a: Use **Kahn's Algorithm** for topological sorting. Start with all zero-indegree nodes, pop from a queue, and reduce indegrees of neighbors.

questions.q: Graph Valid Tree: Check whether an undirected graph forms a valid tree.
questions.a: A valid tree must have exactly `n - 1` edges and be fully connected with no cycles. Use DFS, BFS, or union-find to verify the conditions.

questions.q: Word Ladder: Find the length of the shortest transformation sequence from begin word to end word.
questions.a: Use **BFS** because it naturally finds the shortest number of transformations. Preprocessing wildcard patterns or generating neighbor words efficiently is key to passing large tests.

questions.q: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array: Return the minimum element in a rotated sorted array.
questions.a: Use **binary search**. Compare the middle value with the right boundary to decide whether the minimum lies on the left or right side.

questions.q: Search in Rotated Sorted Array: Search for a target in a rotated sorted array.
questions.a: Apply binary search while determining which half is sorted at each step. Then decide whether the target lies inside that half or the other half.

questions.q: Koko Eating Bananas: Find the minimum eating speed needed to finish piles within `h` hours.
questions.a: Binary-search the answer space on eating speed. For each trial speed, compute the total hours needed and adjust the search boundaries accordingly.

questions.q: Search a 2D Matrix: Determine whether a target exists in a row-wise sorted matrix.
questions.a: Treat the matrix like a flattened sorted array and perform binary search using index math to map a middle position back to row and column.

questions.q: Time Based Key-Value Store: Design a structure that stores values with timestamps and retrieves the latest value at or before a timestamp.
questions.a: Store a sorted list of `[timestamp, value]` for each key, then use **binary search** to find the rightmost timestamp less than or equal to the query timestamp.

questions.q: Median of Two Sorted Arrays: Find the median of two sorted arrays in logarithmic time.
questions.a: Use binary search on partitions of the smaller array so that the combined left half and right half are balanced. This is a well-known hard interview problem.

questions.q: Combination Sum: Return all unique combinations of numbers that add up to a target, where each number can be reused.
questions.a: Use **backtracking**. At each step, choose the current candidate again or move to the next one. Track the running sum and stop when it exceeds the target.

questions.q: Subsets: Return all possible subsets of a given array.
questions.a: Use backtracking or iterative subset building. At each index, branch into including the element or excluding it. This is a standard recursion puzzle.

questions.q: Permutations: Return all permutations of a list of distinct numbers.
questions.a: Use backtracking with a `used` array or in-place swapping. This is a classic interview recursion problem and a good way to explain DFS state trees.

questions.q: Word Search: Determine whether a word exists in a 2D board by moving horizontally or vertically.
questions.a: Run DFS from each starting cell and mark visited cells during the current path so they are not reused. Backtrack after exploring each direction.

questions.q: Generate Parentheses: Generate all valid combinations of `n` pairs of parentheses.
questions.a: Use backtracking with counts of open and close brackets used so far. Add `(` if open count is below `n`, and add `)` only if close count is less than open count.

questions.q: Daily Temperatures: For each day, return how many days you must wait until a warmer temperature.
questions.a: Use a **monotonic decreasing stack** of indices. When a warmer temperature appears, resolve all previous colder days from the stack.

questions.q: Valid Parentheses: Determine whether a string of brackets is valid.
questions.a: Use a **stack** and push opening brackets. For every closing bracket, ensure it matches the latest opening bracket. This is a foundational coding question.

questions.q: Min Stack: Design a stack that supports retrieving the minimum element in constant time.
questions.a: Maintain a second stack that tracks the minimum value at each level, or store pairs of `[value, currentMin]`. Both `push` and `pop` remain **O(1)**.

questions.q: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation: Evaluate an expression given in postfix notation.
questions.a: Use a stack. Push numbers, and whenever an operator appears, pop the top two operands, apply the operation, and push the result back.

questions.q: Car Fleet: Count how many car fleets arrive at the destination.
questions.a: Sort cars by starting position from nearest to farthest from the destination, compute each car's arrival time, and use a monotonic idea to merge cars into fleets.

questions.q: Largest Rectangle in Histogram: Find the largest rectangle area in a histogram.
questions.a: Use a **monotonic increasing stack** to find the width where each bar is the limiting height. This is a famous hard stack problem asked in strong interviews.

questions.q: Longest Consecutive Sequence: Find the length of the longest consecutive integer sequence in an unsorted array.
questions.a: Put all numbers in a `Set`, then only start counting from numbers that do not have a predecessor. This avoids repeated work and gives **O(n)** time.
